messages.author: 5a91d3696b12d600
messages.subject: calling rates not independent
parts:
I am modeling bobwhite abundance using removal sampling (5 successive 1-minute counts per site) and it is apparent that, if 1 bird calls it elicits a response from nearby birds.  Thus, detection probabilities are inflated if 1 or more birds are calling.  Is it reasonable to use the total number of birds detected at a site as a covariate for p?  I've tried it and the delta AIC is very good but I am worried that this may be because I am using a product of detection (number of birds detected at a site) to estimate detection rates.  I thought about the negative binomial but it is not the birds that are overdispersed, only their calling rates.  Other suggestions?
Thanks!
Joe

messages.author: 4a15de51da4445ae
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] calling rates not independent
parts:
hi Joe,
no, it doesn't seem reasonable to do that because the binary observation and the count are both , essentially, the same dependent variable. So you're kind of regressing y on a version of itself, if I understand what you're saying.
Maybe you could model the total detections or unique individuals as a binomial count?
Alternatively: maybe a behavioral response model -- the pr(detection) increases after the first detection -- would account for this at least in part?
regards
andy
